subject: Banking
title: BCCI: The World's Crooked Bank
description: A quick, practical guide to BCCI: The World's Crooked Bank.

hook.text: BCCI operated in 78 countries and laundered money for drug cartels, terrorists, and dictators.

buildup.text: Founded in 1972, BCCI grew rapidly by offering unusually high returns.

discovery.text: BCCI was a Ponzi scheme. New deposits paid old depositors' returns.

twist.text: BCCI bribed politicians and regulators in multiple countries.

climax.text: When BCCI collapsed in 1991, $20 billion disappeared. It proved that global banks need global oversight.

punchline.text: 78 countries. Drug money. Arms deals. $20 billion gone.

quiz.question: Why was BCCI able to operate corruptly for so long?
options: It was too small to notice
Operating across 78 countries meant no single regulator could see everything

details.summary: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International was a $20 billion global bank that operated as a criminal enterprise, laundering money for drug cartels, dictators, and terrorists while bribing regulators across 73 countries.
details.whyItMatters: BCCI exposed the dangers of a bank operating across dozens of jurisdictions with no single regulator having a complete picture. Its closure triggered reforms in international banking supervision.
takeaways: BCCI operated in 73 countries with no effective consolidated supervision
Clients included the CIA, Pablo Escobar, Saddam Hussein, and Abu Nidal
The bank was shut down simultaneously in seven countries in 1991

faq.question: How did BCCI operate as a criminal enterprise for so long?
faq.answer: BCCI deliberately structured itself across multiple jurisdictions so no single regulator could see the full picture. It was incorporated in Luxembourg, headquartered in London, and audited by two different firms for different divisions.

faq.question: What reforms resulted from the BCCI scandal?
faq.answer: The Basel Committee established requirements for consolidated supervision of international banks. Regulators gained authority to prevent banks from operating in structures designed to avoid oversight, and information sharing between supervisors improved.
